rx_flow.text: Walk me through how your receiver turns a falling edge on the serial line into a byte on its output stream.

answer_key.point: When idle, a low level on the registered serial input starts reception: it loads a countdown of about half a bit period, sets the bit counter and marks itself busy.
Half a bit later it re-checks the start bit and abandons reception if the line has gone high again, which rejects glitches.
Each data bit is sampled once per bit period (8 x prescale clock cycles) and shifted in least-significant bit first.
At the stop bit, if the line is high the byte is copied to the output register and valid is raised; if it is low a frame error is flagged instead.
The serial input is registered before it is used.

misconceptions: Oversamples each bit and takes a majority vote; it samples each bit once, near its middle.
Buffers received bytes in a FIFO; there is a single output register.
Shifts bits in MSB first; it shifts LSB first.
follow_ups: What would happen if a noise spike pulled the line low for just a few clock cycles?
How would you add buffering between the receiver and whatever consumes its bytes?

rx_overrun.text: What happens if a new byte finishes arriving before whatever is downstream has taken the previous one?

answer_key.point: The new byte overwrites the output register: there is no FIFO, so the unread byte is lost.
An overrun error is raised when a byte completes while the previous byte is still marked valid.
The error outputs are one-cycle pulses: they are cleared on every clock, so something must catch them in that cycle.
Valid only drops when the consumer completes the handshake (valid and ready both high).

misconceptions: The receiver applies backpressure on the serial line; there is no flow control.
The overrun flag stays set until cleared; it is a one-cycle pulse.
The new byte is dropped and the old one kept; the new byte overwrites the old one.
follow_ups: How would software find out that a byte was lost?
What would you change so that no byte is ever silently overwritten?

tx_flow.text: Walk me through what your transmitter does from the moment it accepts a byte until the line is idle again.

answer_key.point: When idle and the input is valid, it latches the byte with a stop bit appended, drives the line low for the start bit and loads the bit counter.
Each bit lasts 8 x prescale clock cycles, timed by a down-counter.
Bits are shifted out least-significant bit first.
Ready is held low while a bit period is counting down, so no new byte is accepted mid-frame.
It finishes by driving the stop bit high, then returns to idle with ready raised.

misconceptions: Sends the most significant bit first; it sends the least significant bit first.
Has a transmit FIFO and can queue several bytes; it holds one byte at a time.
follow_ups: How would you let the transmitter accept the next byte without waiting for the stop bit to finish?
What would you change to support a parity bit?

error_pulses.text: Why did you make the receiver's error indicators one-cycle pulses instead of sticky flags that stay set until someone clears them?

answer_key.point: Overrun and frame errors are cleared on every clock and only pulse for a single cycle.
There is no clear or acknowledge input: the module only exposes the error outputs.
The error outputs are driven straight from those registers.

misconceptions: The flags are sticky until software clears them; they are one-cycle pulses.
There is a register interface for status; there is none in this module.
follow_ups: How would a slow microcontroller reliably notice a frame error with this design?
Where would you add sticky status bits if you needed them?

cases.question: rx_flow
cases.answer: When the line is idle and I see the registered RX input go low, I treat that as a possible start bit: I load the prescale counter with about half a bit time, set the bit counter for the start, data and stop bits, and set busy. When that half-bit countdown expires I'm in the middle of the start bit, so I check the line again; if it's back high it was a glitch and I abort. Otherwise every full bit period, which is eight times the prescale value in clock cycles, I sample the line once and shift the bit into the data register from the top, so the byte comes in LSB first. At the stop bit I check that the line is high; if so I copy the byte to the output register and raise tvalid, and if the stop bit is low I flag a frame error and drop the byte.

cases.question: rx_flow
cases.answer: Um so basically the RX side sits waiting and the moment the wire drops low it kind of arms itself, it waits like half a bit so it lands in the middle of that start bit, and double checks it's actually still low, because if not it was just noise and it goes back to waiting. Then it just ticks along one bit time at a time and grabs a sample in the middle of each bit, pushing it in so the first bit ends up as the lowest bit of the byte. And at the end it looks at the stop bit, if that's high the byte gets published on the stream side with valid set, and if it's low that's a framing problem so it raises the frame error instead of handing the byte over.

cases.question: rx_flow
cases.answer: When the line goes low it starts counting using the prescale value, and then it samples each bit and shifts them into a register. Once it has all eight bits it puts the byte on the output and sets valid.

cases.question: rx_flow
cases.answer: It's a pretty standard UART receiver. It detects the start bit, samples the data at the configured baud rate, and then outputs the received byte on the AXI stream interface. It follows the usual UART protocol, so nothing too unusual there.

cases.question: rx_flow
cases.answer: The receiver oversamples at sixteen times the baud rate and takes a majority vote of three samples in the middle of each bit, which makes it robust to noise. Bits come in most significant bit first, and the completed byte goes into a small FIFO so the consumer can read it later.

cases.question: rx_overrun
cases.answer: There's no buffering on the output, it's a single register, so if a new byte completes while the old one is still valid, the new byte just overwrites it and the old one is gone. The receiver notices that case because when it writes the new byte it sets the overrun error from the old valid flag. But that error flag, like the frame error, only goes high for one clock cycle, because I clear both at the start of every cycle, so whatever is watching has to latch it.

cases.question: rx_overrun
cases.answer: In that case the receiver holds onto the old byte and ignores the new one until the consumer reads it, so nothing gets overwritten. It also sets the overrun flag and keeps it set until the module is reset, so software can check it whenever it wants.

cases.question: tx_flow
cases.answer: So when it's idle it has ready high, and as soon as valid shows up it grabs the byte, tacks a stop bit onto the top of it and pulls the TX line low for the start bit. Then for each bit it counts down eight times the prescale, and every time the count runs out it shifts the next bit out, lowest bit first. While it's counting, ready stays low so nobody can push another byte in the middle. After the last data bit it drives the line high for the stop bit and then goes back to idle with ready up again.

cases.question: error_pulses
cases.answer: I kept them as single-cycle pulses mostly to keep the receiver tiny and purely event-driven: the core clears both error flags every clock and doesn't have any clear or acknowledge input, so there's no extra state or register interface. If a design needs sticky errors, the wrapper or the software side can latch the pulse into a status register and clear it on read. The trade-off is that if nothing samples them on that exact cycle you lose the event, so you can't just poll them from slow software.

cases.question: error_pulses
cases.answer: I made the error flags sticky so software can poll them whenever it wants. They stay set until you write to the clear bit in the control register, which means you never miss an error.

cases.question: error_pulses
cases.answer: I made the error flags sticky so software can poll them whenever it wants. They stay set until the module is reset.

follow_ups.prompt: Look again at how those flags behave from one clock to the next. Why would you build them that way?
follow_ups.answer: Oh, actually they get cleared at the start of every clock, so they're one-cycle pulses, not sticky. I kept it that way so the receiver stays tiny with no clear or acknowledge input; if software needs sticky errors a wrapper can latch the pulse into a status register, but if nothing samples it on that cycle the event is lost.
